name: Olga Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt. I run a D10 dozer at a bauxite mine, open pit, about forty minutes out of town. Bauxite's the red rock they make aluminium from, and it sits in a shallow layer, so my job is clearing the topsoil off ahead of the diggers, ripping the hard bits, and keeping the haul roads and the dumps tidy. Ten-hour day shifts, five on, two off. I like that I can look back at the end of the day and see a flat, clean bench where there was a mess, and I hate the red dust, it gets in your ears, your bra, your sandwiches.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Rui, he's an electrician at the refinery down the coast. I bought a small apartment in town when I was twenty-four with my first big bonus and I rent it out, so between that and what's in the bank I'm comfortable. My dad has a little earthmoving business back home, farm dams and driveways, that's where I learned to run a dozer at fifteen. I don't really do the AI thing. I've got a phone for calls and the weather, that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much, I'm not a big talker about this stuff. If someone at the tea break brought it up, I'd say, see, nothing to worry about. I'm not online except to look at dozer videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing, which suits me. Even with AI as hype, I know they're trialling remote dozers at another site, but that's slow and patchy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going to work, keep the apartment rented, keep the money where it is. I'd maybe pay a chunk off the apartment loan early because I don't like owing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Normal. Like hearing the forecast's the same as yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned remote dozers at another site. What have you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A guy I did my tickets with, Brendan, works there. He says they've got two dozers you drive from a container with screens, and they spend half the time stuck because the camera can't tell mud from rock. A dozer's all feel. You feel the blade bite through your seat. A camera doesn't have a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd stay clear of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, as long as I can. If they made me do it, I'd do it, I'm not stupid. But I wouldn't put my hand up.

S0.say: She wouldn't say much, just tell the crew at the tea break that there's nothing to worry about. She's not online except to watch dozer videos.
S0.think: She thinks she keeps doing what she does, which suits her. Remote dozers being trialled at another site would stay slow and patchy.
S0.do: Keeps working, keeps her apartment rented and her savings where they are. Pays a chunk off the apartment loan early because she dislikes owing money.
S0.feel: Fine and normal, like a forecast that's the same as yesterday.
S0.quote: A dozer's all feel. You feel the blade bite through your seat. A camera doesn't have a seat.
S0.fieldNote: Olga is short-spoken and practical; her confidence rests on the physical feel of the machine, which she believes cameras can't copy. She'd go remote only if made to. Her money instinct is to reduce debt rather than invest more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, well, we'll see what sticks. Some things'll work, some won't, like every new gadget they bring in. I wouldn't get worked up in front of people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think dozers are a bit harder to automate than trucks, so I've got longer than the truck drivers. But the dozers might go remote, and I don't want to sit in a container. There are plenty of other mines round here, so if this one goes all screens I'd move to one that hasn't yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep an eye out. If our site announced remote dozers, I'd start ringing round the other mines to see who's still running them with people on board. I'd keep saving like I do now, a bit more maybe, and I'd keep the apartment as my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a noise in the engine you can't place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move mines rather than learn the remote setup. Why that way round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good at the thing I do, and I've seen what happens to people who switch to the new thing too early. My dad bought the first laser grader in our district and spent two years fixing it instead of working. I'm not doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Rui see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, he thinks I'm being a dinosaur. He's an electrician, he likes gadgets. We just don't talk about it at dinner, that's easier.

S1.say: She'd tell people at work 'we'll see what sticks', like every new gadget the company brings in. She wouldn't get worked up in front of anyone.
S1.think: She thinks dozers are harder to automate than trucks, giving her longer than the truck drivers. If her site went remote she'd move to a mine nearby that still runs dozers with people in them.
S1.do: Keeps working and watches for announcements; if remote dozers came to her site, starts ringing other mines still using crewed machines. Saves a little more and keeps the apartment as her safety net.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, like an engine noise she can't place yet.
S1.quote: My dad bought the first laser grader in our district and spent two years fixing it instead of working. I'm not doing that.
S1.fieldNote: Her plan for change is to move to a mine that hasn't changed yet; the plentiful local jobs make that realistic for now. Her dad's bad experience with the first laser grader shapes her caution. She and Rui disagree and simply avoid the topic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and someone should slow it down. Not ban it, I'm not one of those, but you can't flip a whole country in two years. At work I'd just say keep your head down and see what the company says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think that's me done. If the robot can feel the blade as well as I can, there's no mine I can move to that hasn't got one. I'm twenty-seven, I've got the apartment and savings, so I wouldn't starve, but I'd have no idea what I'd do every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big, we were looking at a new four-wheel drive and that'd be off. I'd sit down with Rui and work out how long the rent from the apartment plus savings would last us, probably a couple of years. I'd talk to Dad about whether there's any work in his business, but if robots are doing dams too there won't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty bad. Like the ground under the dozer going soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your dad. What do you think he'd say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say come home and we'll work it out, that's what he always says. But Dad's little business is two dozers and an excavator. A robot company wouldn't even notice it on the way past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do in the two years before it fully arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work every overtime shift they'd give me and put it all away. I don't know what else you'd do with two years, honestly. It's not enough to learn a whole new trade, and I wouldn't know which one.

S2.say: She'd say it's mad and someone should slow it down, without banning it, because a country can't change in two years. At work she'd tell people to keep their heads down and wait for the company.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be finished, because there'd be no mine left without robots to move to. Her apartment and savings mean she wouldn't starve, but she'd have no idea what to do each day.
S2.do: Cancels the planned four-wheel drive, works out with Rui how long apartment rent and savings would last, and asks her dad about work in his business. Takes every overtime shift in the two years before and saves it all.
S2.feel: Pretty bad, like the ground under the dozer going soft.
S2.quote: But Dad's little business is two dozers and an excavator. A robot company wouldn't even notice it on the way past.
S2.fieldNote: Her main safety valve, moving to another mine, disappears in this picture, which is why she jumps to alarmed. She sees no point retraining in two years because she can't name a trade that would survive. Her father's offer of help is warm but she doubts it would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'd better start planning, but I wouldn't be shouting about it. I'd want the government and the companies to sit down and work out something sensible for mining towns. Nothing crazy, just a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd keep working most of those five years. By the end I'd be thirty-two and in trouble, but I'd have a bit more saved and the apartment paid off. It's the same ending, just with a bit more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year I'd throw extra at the apartment loan so it's paid off by 2029, then the rent is pure income. I'd keep doing the dozer as long as they'd have me and save a bit more each month. I might look at a second small property if prices stayed sensible, because rent seems to be the one thing a robot can't take off me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more a slow worry than a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years buy you, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mainly getting the loan off the apartment. Two years, I'm still owing the bank when it hits. Five years, I own the roof over somebody's head outright, and that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about training for something new with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I'd want to see what's actually left first. I'm not going to spend money on a course for some job that's gone by the time I finish. I'd rather wait and see what people still need humans for.

S3.say: She'd say it's time to start planning, without shouting about it. She'd want government and companies to work out a sensible plan for mining towns.
S3.think: She thinks she'd keep working most of the five years and be in trouble by thirty-two. It's the same ending, just with more in the bank and the apartment paid off.
S3.do: Puts extra money into the apartment loan to clear it by 2029 and keeps working the dozer while saving more. Considers buying a second small rental if prices stay sensible.
S3.feel: Anxious in a slow, steady way rather than shocked.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm still owing the bank when it hits. Five years, I own the roof over somebody's head outright, and that's something.
S3.fieldNote: For Olga, extra time translates mainly into paying off the apartment; rent is the one income she thinks robots can't touch. She won't retrain until she sees what jobs remain. Her centre outlook shows in calls for a 'sensible' plan rather than blame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, people shouldn't panic. I'd tell younger ones on the crew to start thinking about what they'd do next. I'd be fairly calm about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. I'd do eight or so more years on the dozer, have the apartment paid off, maybe a second one, and be thirty-seven with some money behind me. I still don't know what I'd do after, but there'd be time to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working and paying off the apartment in the first couple of years. Around year five, I'd look properly at going into Dad's business and maybe taking it over, doing smaller jobs for farmers, the kind of fiddly work big robot companies won't bother with. I wouldn't do anything with AI myself, but I'd watch what the other mines are doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier a robot company wouldn't notice Dad's business. Why does it seem possible here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with ten years, I'd have time to see if anyone actually bothers with the small stuff. Farmers out our way don't trust anything they haven't seen work for three seasons. That's ten years of work right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if it went badly for mining towns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know if it's anyone's fault, really. Companies do what's cheapest, that's what companies are. I'd blame the government if it had ten years and still did nothing.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long time and nobody should panic. She'd tell younger crewmates to start thinking about what comes next and stay calm in public.
S4.think: She thinks ten years feels manageable: eight more years on the dozer, the apartment paid off, maybe a second one, and money behind her at thirty-seven. She doesn't know what comes after but there'd be time to find out.
S4.do: Keeps working and pays off the apartment in the first couple of years. Around year five, looks seriously at joining and possibly taking over her dad's earthmoving business doing small farm jobs, while watching what other mines do.
S4.quote: Farmers out our way don't trust anything they haven't seen work for three seasons. That's ten years of work right there.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years her dad's small business comes back as a real option, built on her belief that cautious farmers will be slow to trust robots. She doesn't blame companies for chasing cost but would blame a government that wasted a decade. She still has no intention of using AI herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's nowhere to move to and no time to pay anything off. What would help is honest notice from the company, like a date, so I can plan, and some sort of payout that matches the years you've put in. I don't need anyone to save me. I just want to know the date, so I'm not the last one on the bench when they switch the lights off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask Rui, he'd give you the opposite answers to me on everything. That's how we stay together, I think.

headlineQuote: I don't need anyone to save me. I just want to know the date, so I'm not the last one on the bench when they switch the lights off.
portrait: Olga is a 27-year-old dozer operator at an open-pit bauxite mine who lives with her partner Rui, a refinery electrician, and owns a small rental apartment. She learned to run a dozer at fifteen in her dad's earthmoving business, trusts the physical feel of the machine and never uses AI. Her instinct with change is to move to a mine that hasn't changed yet and to pay off debt, not to retrain. Fast AGI alarms her because there'd be nowhere left to move; with ten years she can picture taking over her dad's small business doing farm jobs.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no other mine to move to and no time to pay off her apartment.
whatWouldHelp: Honest notice of a date from the company so she can plan, and a payout that matches the years she's put in.
